chunks.text: The bottlebrush commonly grown in Indian gardens is usually the crimson or common red bottlebrush, scientifically Melaleuca citrina — the name it was formally given in 1802 by French botanist Georges Louis Marie Dumont de Courset, though many herbaria (including some in Australia) still use the older name Callistemon citrinus. It belongs to the myrtle family, Myrtaceae; the epithet 'citrina' refers to the lemon-like scent of its crushed leaves. The species is endemic to eastern Australia — coastal New South Wales (including the Blue Mountains) and the east coast of Victoria — where it grows naturally in swamps and along creeks and rivers. It is a hardy shrub usually 1-3 m tall (occasionally to 5 m), with alternately arranged leaves 26-99 mm long bearing visible oil glands and 7-26 parallel veins. Its distinctive flower spikes carry up to 80 individual flowers each, with 30-45 red-filamented, purple-anthered stamens per flower, blooming mainly in November-December in its native range but often through much of the year in cultivation; the woody, cup-shaped seed capsules stay closed on the branch until the plant or that branch dies.

Bottlebrush is grown almost entirely as an ornamental — it has been in cultivation since 1794, is easily propagated from seed or cuttings, tolerates drought and frost, and does well in sunny positions in most soils, with popular cultivars including 'Splendens', 'Firebrand' and 'White Anzac'. Its real ecological value is as a nectar source: in Australia it feeds honeyeaters such as the eastern spinebill, New Holland honeyeater, noisy miner and red wattlebird, plus silvereyes, while crimson rosellas eat its seed, and its long flowering season also supports honeybees. One historically notable specimen grown in England was raised from material collected at Botany Bay by Joseph Banks during James Cook's first voyage in 1770, making it one of the earliest Australian plants ever cultivated outside its homeland. The species also has an indirect agricultural legacy: the herbicide mesotrione is a synthetic analogue of leptospermone, a natural herbicidal compound produced by this plant's roots.
